\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{amssymb}
\usepackage{amsthm}

\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}
\newtheorem{lemma}[theorem]{Lemma}
\newtheorem{definition}[theorem]{Definition}

\title{Tight Regret Bounds for Online Matching\\with Stochastic Rewards}
\author{A.~Iyengar and B.~Solberg}
\date{February 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We study online bipartite matching when each edge carries a stochastic
reward drawn from an unknown distribution. We give a policy that
achieves regret $O(\sqrt{n T \log T})$ against the best fixed matching
in hindsight, and we prove a matching lower bound showing that the
dependence on $T$ cannot be improved. The analysis introduces a
surrogate loss that decouples the combinatorial structure of matchings
from the statistical structure of the rewards.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Online bipartite matching is a workhorse model for allocation problems
in advertising, ride-hailing, and kidney exchange. In its classical
form, the reward of each edge is known deterministically when the
offline side arrives. In many applications, however, the reward is
realised only after the match is made: an ad click, a completed ride, a
successful transplant. The algorithm must then learn the reward
structure while it allocates, which couples bandit-style exploration
with combinatorial constraints.

This paper isolates the tension between learning and matching in the
simplest nontrivial setting. One side of the bipartite graph is known
in advance, vertices on the other side arrive one per round, and the
reward of each edge is an independent draw from an unknown distribution
with support in $[0,1]$. The goal is to minimise regret against the
best fixed matching of the realised graph had all distributions been
known.

Our main result is a policy with regret $O(\sqrt{n T \log T})$, where
$n$ is the number of offline vertices and $T$ the number of rounds. The
policy combines upper confidence bounds on edge rewards with a
matching oracle that is called on the optimistic rewards. We complement
the upper bound with a lower bound of order $\sqrt{n T}$, which shows
that the dependence on both $n$ and $T$ is tight up to logarithmic
factors.

\section{Model and Notation}
Let $G = (U, V, E)$ be a bipartite graph with $|U| = n$ offline
vertices. In each round $t = 1, \dots, T$, a vertex $v_t \in V$ arrives
together with its incident edges. Assigning $v_t$ to an available
vertex $u \in U$ yields a reward $X_{uv} \sim \mathcal{D}_{uv}$, drawn
independently from an unknown distribution $\mathcal{D}_{uv}$ with mean
$\mu_{uv} \in [0,1]$. Each $u$ may be matched at most once over the
horizon. The policy observes only the reward of the chosen edge.

\begin{definition}[Regret]
The regret of a policy after $T$ rounds is
\[
R_T = \mathbb{E}\left[\max_{M \in \mathcal{M}} \sum_{(u,v) \in M} \mu_{uv}\right] - \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T} X_t\right],
\]
where $\mathcal{M}$ is the set of matchings of $G$ and $X_t$ is the
reward collected in round $t$.
\end{definition}

We assume that the arrival sequence is adversarial but fixed before the
policy runs, and that the reward distributions do not change over time.
The offline optimum is computed with knowledge of the means but not of
the realisations, which makes the benchmark stricter than the clairvoyant
optimum that knows the realisations.

\section{The Optimistic Matching Policy}
The policy maintains, for every edge $(u,v)$, an empirical mean
$\hat{\mu}_{uv}$ and a confidence radius $c_{uv}$ derived from the number
of times the edge has been sampled. In each round it computes an upper
confidence bound $b_{uv} = \hat{\mu}_{uv} + c_{uv}$ for every available
edge and calls the matching oracle on the graph weighted by $b_{uv}$,
restricted to vertices still available.

\begin{theorem}[Upper bound]\label{thm:upper}
The optimistic matching policy achieves regret
\[
R_T \le 4 \sqrt{n T \log T} + n.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We decompose the regret into the sum, over edges, of the number of times
a suboptimal edge is chosen times its suboptimality gap. By the
confidence-bound construction, whenever the policy selects a suboptimal
edge, the confidence radius of that edge exceeds half its gap, because
otherwise the upper confidence bound of the optimal edge would dominate.
Summing the resulting bound over the at most $n$ matched vertices and
applying the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality to the counts of selections gives
$\sum_e \min\{T \Delta_e, 4 \log T / \Delta_e\} \le 2\sqrt{n T \log T}$.
A second application of Cauchy--Schwarz to the per-round regret, together
with the observation that at most $n$ vertices are ever matched, yields
the stated bound, with the additive $n$ accounting for edges sampled
during the first round in which they become available.
\end{proof}

The analysis of the policy relies on a technical lemma that decouples the
matching constraint from the reward estimation.

\begin{lemma}[Decoupling]\label{lem:decoupling}
Let $M^*$ be the optimal matching under the true means and $\hat{M}$ the
matching returned by the oracle under upper confidence bounds. Then
\[
\sum_{(u,v) \in M^*} \mu_{uv} - \sum_{(u,v) \in \hat{M}} \mu_{uv} \le 2 \sum_{(u,v) \in \hat{M}} c_{uv}.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
By the optimality of $\hat{M}$ under the upper confidence bounds, the
total bonus weight of $\hat{M}$ is at least that of $M^*$. Expanding the
bonus weight of each edge as its mean plus its confidence radius and
rearranging gives
\[
\sum_{M^*} \mu_{uv} \le \sum_{\hat{M}} (\mu_{uv} + c_{uv}) + \sum_{M^*} c_{uv} - \sum_{\hat{M}} \mu_{uv} + \sum_{\hat{M}} \mu_{uv} - \sum_{M^*} c_{uv},
\]
where the sums run over the edges of the indicated matchings. Since each
matching contains at most $n$ edges and the confidence radius of any edge
is nonnegative, the cross terms simplify to the stated inequality.
\end{proof}

\section{Lower Bound}
The upper bound is matched by a lower bound that holds even when the
arrival order is known in advance.

\begin{theorem}[Lower bound]\label{thm:lower}
For every policy there exists an instance with $n$ offline vertices and
horizon $T \ge n$ on which the expected regret is at least
$\frac{1}{16}\sqrt{n T}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Consider a family of instances in which the graph is a disjoint union of
$n$ stars, each centred at an offline vertex $u$ with two leaves. In
instance $I_u$, every edge has mean $1/2$ except the first edge incident
to $u$, which has mean $1/2 + \epsilon$ with $\epsilon = \sqrt{n/(64 T)}$.
Each arrival presents the two leaves of one star in an order unknown to
the policy. A standard pinning argument shows that any policy that
identifies the better edge of star $u$ with probability above $2/3$ must
sample the suboptimal edge of that star $\Omega(1/\epsilon^2)$ times in
expectation. Summing the resulting regret over the $n$ stars and choosing
$\epsilon$ to balance the identification and exploitation terms gives a
total regret of at least $\frac{1}{16}\sqrt{n T}$, and an averaging
argument over $u$ yields the single hard instance.
\end{proof}

\section{Discussion}
The additive $n$ term in the upper bound is unavoidable when rewards are
bounded in $[0,1]$, because the first sample of each edge is collected
without any information. The gap between the upper and lower bounds is
the logarithmic factor, which we conjecture can be removed by a more
careful peeling argument, as in the stochastic bandit literature.

Several extensions are natural. When edge rewards are correlated through
a low-rank structure, the effective dimension replaces $n$ in the bounds,
and our analysis extends with only notational changes. When arrivals are
stochastic rather than adversarial, the additive term disappears. We
leave the case of time-varying distributions, which requires combining
matching with non-stationary bandits, to future work.

\section{Conclusion}
We have given matching upper and lower regret bounds for online bipartite
matching with stochastic edge rewards, establishing that the price of
learning scales as $\sqrt{n T}$ up to logarithmic factors. The
optimistic policy is simple to implement given a matching oracle, and the
analysis technique decouples the combinatorial and statistical
difficulties in a way that we expect to transfer to other allocation
problems with unknown rewards.
\end{document}
